point_one.role: Add the missing sleep-architecture layer: circadian timing may make the later part of the night more wakeable, but the sleep stage at that moment affects how easily awakening breaks through and how groggy it feels.
point_one.new_listener_takeaway: A pre-alarm awakening is not only a clock-timing event; it may be helped by the normal late-night shift away from deep slow-wave sleep toward lighter NREM and REM sleep. Waking from deep N3 and waking from lighter sleep are therefore different experiences, even if they occur at the same scheduled time.
point_one.evidence_anchor: F002 reports that NREM and REM alternate roughly every 90–110 minutes, with less slow-wave sleep and more REM later in the night; F013 and F014 link awakening from deep N3 with greater sleep inertia than awakening from lighter sleep or N2.
point_one.why_it_matters: This gives listeners a concrete reason why the same alarm can be easy to beat on one morning and difficult to beat on another, without requiring the body to predict the exact minute. It also helps them distinguish waking easily from waking with evidence of precise time prediction.
point_one.must_not_overlap_with_full_story: Do not repeat the Main Story’s discussion of the roughly 24-hour body clock, light and regular schedules, pre-waking ACTH or cortisol, brain and heart changes, self-awakening studies, or the 201-person cortisol study. This Point should also avoid restating the conclusion that the body prepares before waking but cannot yet be said to predict an alarm exactly.
point_one.must_not_overlap_with_other_point: Do not discuss repeated self-awakening practice, chronotype, or the 82% and 10.3% findings; those are the focus of Point Two.

point_two.role: Reframe the experience as an individual and potentially trainable sleep habit, using evidence about repeated practice and morningness rather than adding another physiological mechanism.
point_two.new_listener_takeaway: In an 11-person home study, self-awakening success reached 82% on the seventh day after a week of trying, while a separate survey found that only 10.3% of students reported a daily self-awakening habit and that these students kept schedules about 30 minutes earlier. This suggests that consistent intention and a morning-type routine may help some people develop the ability, rather than it being a universal feature of the human body.
point_two.evidence_anchor: F007 reports an 82% success rate on day seven after one week of attempted self-awakening; F004 reports 66 of 643 students, or 10.3%, with a self-awakening habit and an approximately 30-minute earlier schedule associated with morningness.
point_two.why_it_matters: This gives listeners a concrete explanation for why the experience may cluster in certain people and become more reliable with routine. It shifts the useful question from “Can humans predict an alarm?” to “Has this person developed a stable, expected wake-up pattern?”
point_two.must_not_overlap_with_full_story: Do not repeat the Main Story’s general account of light and regular schedules, the ACTH rise about one hour before waking, the 15-man brain-activity study, the short-nap heart-rate finding, the 17-study review, or the 201-adult cortisol result. Point Two should add evidence about individual differences and repeated practice instead.
point_two.must_not_overlap_with_other_point: Do not explain late-night changes in sleep stages, N3-related sleep inertia, or the role of lighter sleep and REM in ease of awakening; those are the focus of Point One.

【既に確定済みのMain Story本文(実際にこの内容が記事に使われます)】
You set your alarm for seven. But before it rings, your eyes open.

For some people, this feels almost magical. Did the body clock know the exact time? Research suggests a more careful answer. The body may be keeping time, while also preparing for a wake-up that it expects.

The human body has a daily clock that follows a roughly 24-hour rhythm. Light is an important signal for this clock. A regular pattern of sleeping and waking can also help keep it on schedule. This timing system can prepare the body for morning, but that does not mean it can always predict one alarm perfectly.

Researchers have found signs of preparation before planned waking. In one laboratory study, people were led to expect that their sleep would end at a certain time. A hormone called ACTH began to rise about one hour before waking. The researchers said this rise may reflect both the daily body clock and a preparation process for the end of sleep.

Other studies looked at “self-awakening,” when people try to wake at a planned time without outside help. In one study of 15 healthy men, seven woke within 30 minutes of the planned time. Among those who succeeded, changes in brain activity appeared about 30 minutes before waking. In a small afternoon-nap study, heart rate began to rise about three minutes before waking in the self-awakening condition.

These findings suggest that waking may be a process, not a single moment. The body can begin shifting toward wakefulness before the eyes open.

But there is an important limit. Many self-awakening studies asked participants to aim for a particular time. They did not simply study people who happened to wake just before a ringing alarm. A 2023 review found 17 studies with 715 participants, but the methods and definitions were different. So researchers cannot yet say that the body clock knows the exact alarm time.

A newer study of 201 adults sleeping at home found that cortisol, a body hormone, rose on average before waking and reached its highest level about 36 minutes afterward. But people varied widely, and the study did not find a clear faster rise around the moment of waking.
